title: Impact, reach and value rationale
objective: Compare a broad low-friction lookup and a rare high-risk approval process.
clearance: Rewritten draft; pending SME and partner clearance

blocks.x: Impact is more than how many people a use case touches. It combines reach, frequency, and the business consequence: cost, revenue, risk, or quality.

items: **Consequence:** what happens to cost, revenue, risk, or quality when it goes well or badly.

blocks.x: A workflow used by 200 people twice a day may be a bigger capacity opportunity than a weekly task for five people. But a rare compliance event can still matter a great deal. Record the rationale rather than forcing every impact into a seat count.

High, medium, and low ratings are useful in a workshop, but each needs a short rationale and an evidence status. "High, because about 200 agents do this several times a day (champion's estimate, to confirm with the ticketing data)" is defensible. "High" on its own is not.

items: **Treating addressable users as active users.** Not everyone who could use a capability will.
**Double-counting.** The same saved minutes can't be claimed twice under two benefit lines.
**Monetizing too early.** Use financial modeling only after the assumptions are explicit and labeled.

blocks.x: Glean's value-selling training notes that most use cases deliver multiple value drivers. A complete customer view, for example, can improve both growth and efficiency. Mapping those connections makes a stronger narrative and speaks to several stakeholders at once. It also raises the risk of double counting, so state which driver each number belongs to.

blocks.title: The parts of impact
blocks.alt: Three stacked parts of impact: reach, the number of people affected; frequency, how often the work happens; and consequence, what each occurrence costs in time, quality, or risk.
